rationale: B wins by staying a touch more disciplined about which facts can carry which story: it keeps the actual prompt-to-layout fact as “Figma's AI now draws the layout from a prompt...” and makes the Adobe peg conditional instead of pretending it is automatically warm. A has sharper proof demands, especially “a real exported React component a reporter can inspect and run,” but it also tries to make “The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code” do more than the update supports. That is the difference: B leaves less strategic cleanup before a founder starts picking reporters.
gaps_in_A: “The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code” smuggles production code into the headline; the update only says Make exports React and HTML/CSS, not that anyone ships it.
“The launch is the first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition” invents “first substantive” and over-warms a peg whose date is not supplied.
“AI design assistant generates layouts from a prompt” — calling this `duplicate` throws away the cleanest design-practitioner angle in the update.
“the ‘does AI get its own SKU’ question is being decided across the software category right now” is a useful hypothesis, not a supplied fact.
gaps_in_B: “faster work, fewer hours billed for it” is labor-market seasoning with no proof in the update.
“it lands on 4 million desks” overstates the 4 million-user claim; usage is not availability, adoption, or activation of the assistant.
“expands its addressable seat count” is investor-deck math smuggled into an angle; the update gives pricing, not TAM or buyer expansion.
“a procurement story for every design and engineering org already paying Figma” overclaims buyer impact before seat scope, enterprise terms, or adoption are known.
